title: IAS 2 Reviewer
subject: Information Assurance and Security 2 (ITAS311-T) - 3rd Year 1st Sem
summary: Comprehensive interactive examination covering the reviewer's six lessons: post-audit activities including the exit interview, data analysis, audit reports and presentation of findings (Lessons 3 and 5); log information and security controls from security logging through IDS detection methods, layered defense, NAC, host isolation and system hardening (Lesson 4); the risk management process of identification, assessment, response and monitoring (Lesson 6); business continuity management with RTO, RPO, MTD, BIA, plan review and testing (Lesson 7); and backing up data with incident response preparation, the three-phase response model, post-incident review, documentation and reporting (Lesson 8).

chapters.title: Post-Audit Activities
chapters.description: Covers the definition of post-audit activities, the exit interview (participants, purpose, preparation, advantages and limitations), the five-step data analysis process, the audit report format and qualities, and the presentation of findings, drawing on Lessons 3 and 5.

questions.question: Which statement best describes post-audit activities?
choices: Steps performed to plan and schedule the audit engagement before fieldwork begins.
Actions after an audit to review, analyze, document, and communicate its results.
Controls installed by management to limit access during field testing work.
Procedures used to collect evidence while the audit is in progress.
questions.explanation: Post-audit activities are performed after the audit has been conducted to review, analyze, document, and communicate the results.

questions.question: When is an exit interview normally held?
choices: Before the audit scope and objectives are agreed with the audited entity.
Immediately after the final audit report has been released.
At the conclusion of audit fieldwork, when necessary.
During the initial planning stage of the audit.
questions.explanation: An exit interview is a meeting held at the conclusion of audit fieldwork, when necessary, before the final report is released.

questions.question: What does the Prepare objective of an exit interview accomplish?
choices: It lets the client respond and comment before the final report is issued.
It guarantees that any disputed findings will be removed from the report.
It transfers responsibility for corrective actions to the audit team.
It prevents the audited entity from reviewing the audit evidence.
questions.explanation: The Prepare objective allows the audit client to provide responses and comments before the final report is issued.

questions.question: Which sequence represents the post-audit reporting flow in the reference?
choices: Draft report review, exit interview, management responses, final audit report.
Exit interview, draft report review, final audit report, management responses.
Management responses, final report, exit interview, draft report review.
Exit interview, management responses, draft report review, final audit report.
questions.explanation: The reference sequence is audit fieldwork, exit interview, management responses and comments, draft report review, then final audit report.

questions.question: What is the general purpose of the exit interview?
choices: To discuss findings and clarify concerns before the report is finalized.
To finish all the field testing and evidence collection work for the audit.
To publish the final audit report to the stakeholders.
To set the scope and objectives of the next audit.
questions.explanation: The exit interview gives the auditor and audited entity a chance to discuss findings, clarify concerns, and establish common understanding before the report is finalized.

questions.question: What is the purpose of audit team participation in the exit interview?
choices: To approve the corrective actions that the management proposes.
To audit the meeting as an independent observer.
To present and explain the findings and lead the discussion.
To record the minutes for the audit client's records.
questions.explanation: The audit team, such as the lead auditor, presents and explains the audit findings and facilitates the discussion.

questions.question: What is the main role of the audited entity's management in the exit interview?
choices: To independently verify the audit team's testing methods.
To review the findings and provide context and explanations.
To decide which findings appear in the final report.
To complete the remaining field work on behalf of the auditors.
questions.explanation: Management of the audited entity reviews the findings, provides explanations or additional context, and responds to the issues identified.

questions.question: Who may attend as other participants in an exit interview?
choices: Personnel who are selected by the lead auditor during the meeting.
Regulators required to approve every exit interview.
Consultants hired to conduct the follow-up audit.
People invited by the client to add information or perspective.
questions.explanation: Other participants are individuals invited by the audit client to supply relevant information, clarification, or perspective about the audited processes or findings.

questions.question: Which two questions guide auditors when using the exit interview to close information gaps?
choices: What failed and who is to blame?
Why was the issue missed and how was it discovered?
Who will provide the missing information and when?
How much will the fix cost and who will pay?
questions.explanation: Auditors use the exit interview to identify missing information by asking who is responsible for providing it and when it can be expected.

questions.question: In the reference example, what missing item did the audit team address during the exit interview?
choices: The finance team's reconciled cash position for the quarter.
The IT department's access control and user log reports.
The network team's revised firewall policy for servers.
The HR department's hiring records.
questions.explanation: The example shows the audit team identifying that the IT department had not submitted its latest access-control review or user-permission logs, then asking who will provide them and establishing a deadline.

questions.question: Which is NOT something the reference says to prepare before the auditors leave?
choices: An estimate of the internal approval timeline.
A target date for the final report.
A target date for the draft report.
A revised scope for the next audit cycle.
questions.explanation: The reference lists a target date for the draft report, the approval timeline, and a target date for the final report. Setting a scope for the next audit is not among them.

questions.question: How does the exit interview keep everyone accountable?
choices: By transferring all findings to the final report without discussion.
By setting responsibilities and target dates for open items.
By publishing disagreements before the final report.
By limiting the number of participants in the meeting.
questions.explanation: The exit interview establishes responsibilities and target dates for outstanding items and reporting, which keeps participants accountable.

questions.question: Which advantage explains how the exit interview improves accuracy?
choices: It removes all negative findings from the final report.
It shortens the audit reporting timeline.
It lets the entity correct errors with added context.
It reduces the number of participants involved.
questions.explanation: The exit interview allows the audited entity to provide additional context and correct possible misunderstandings or errors, improving accuracy.

questions.question: Which statement reflects a limitation of the exit interview?
choices: It is held when necessary, not required for every audit.
It is required for every audit without any exception.
It always resolves every disagreement between the parties.
It guarantees that technical findings are understood by all.
questions.explanation: One recorded limitation is that the exit interview is held when necessary rather than being required for every audit.

questions.question: A reviewer finds that technical audit findings are hard for some participants to understand. Which limitation does this illustrate?
choices: Time constraints.
Communication gaps.
Unresolved issues.
Accountability risks.
questions.explanation: The reference lists communication gaps as a limitation because technical audit findings may be difficult for some participants to understand.

questions.question: What happens if differences of opinion remain after the exit interview?
choices: The audit is automatically marked incomplete.
The disputed findings are removed from the final report.
The disagreements are documented in the audit report.
The meeting is repeated until agreement is reached.
questions.explanation: If differences of opinion remain, they may be documented and included in the audit report rather than blocking the audit.

questions.question: What does data analysis mean in the audit context?
choices: The physical inspection of paper and digital records during fieldwork.
The delivery of audit conclusions to management.
The assignment of corrective actions to departments.
Intelligence from reviewing audit data, often with technology.
questions.explanation: Data analysis means the intelligence generated from reviewing audit-related information, often using technology, to find actionable audit insights.

questions.question: Why are focused questions preferred in Step 1 of data analysis?
choices: They point to the analysis needed and relevant data.
They are easier to record than open-ended questions are.
They automatically produce more usable data.
They shorten the executive summary of the report.
questions.explanation: Focused questions, like how metrics changed over time or whether they correlate, help determine the analysis needed and which data is most relevant.

questions.question: Which activity belongs to the data wrangling step?
choices: Defining the questions that guide the analysis.
Searching for outliers and dealing with null values.
Distributing the final report to management.
Interpreting multiple visualizations together with data.
questions.explanation: Data wrangling cleans the data by searching for outliers, dealing with null values, and looking for incorrectly input data.

questions.question: Which analysis type searches for the cause of, and a solution to, an existing problem?
choices: Predictive analysis.
Descriptive analysis.
Diagnostic analysis.
Comparative analysis.
questions.explanation: Diagnostic analysis uses data to search for the cause of, and a solution to, an existing problem.

questions.question: Which analysis type combines historical data and statistical modeling to forecast performance?
choices: Descriptive analysis.
Diagnostic analysis.
Interpretive analysis.
Predictive analysis.
questions.explanation: Predictive analysis combines historical data and statistical modeling to forecast how certain metrics will perform in the future.

questions.question: Which analysis type summarizes key sections in order to describe the data?
choices: Descriptive analysis.
Predictive analysis.
Diagnostic analysis.
Correlation analysis.
questions.explanation: Descriptive analysis is a way to describe the data by summarizing key sections.

questions.question: In Step 5, what does interpreting the results require the analyst to determine?
choices: Which raw files should be deleted after the analysis step.
What is being learned from the results of the analysis.
Which software performed the analysis fastest.
Which metrics were collected during Step 2.
questions.explanation: Step 5 asks what you are learning from the results so the insights can be applied to the business.

questions.question: Which item is a purpose of an audit report?
choices: Reducing the number of audit findings.
Assigning blame for control failures.
Documenting examined evidence.
Automating the audit process.
questions.explanation: The purposes of an audit report include formal communication, documentation of evidence, and initiation of corrective action closure.

questions.question: Which part of the audit report is described as the most critical content?
choices: The introductory paragraph.
The signature of the auditor.
The basis of the opinion.
The opinion of the auditor.
questions.explanation: The auditor's opinion is the most critical content in an audit report because it states the impression derived after auditing the financial statements.

questions.question: What should the title of an audit report mention?
choices: Independent Auditor's Report.
The audit period covered.
The audited entity's address.
The lead auditor's name.
questions.explanation: The reference states the title should mention Independent Auditor's Report.

questions.question: What does the Management's Responsibility section state about the financial statements?
choices: They are prepared by the auditor from management's records.
They are the responsibility of the organization's management.
They are jointly certified by management and the auditor.
They are exempt from financial controls once audited by the firm.
questions.explanation: The section explains that the financial statements are the responsibility of the organization's management, including formulating financial controls and maintaining records to prevent fraud.

questions.question: What do the Standards on Auditing require of the auditor, according to the reference?
choices: Preparation of the financial statements.
Approval of the management's accounting policies.
Full compliance with the ethical requirements.
Certification of the entity's tax filings.
questions.explanation: The audit report is based on Standards on Auditing, which require that the auditor complies with ethical requirements.

questions.question: Which supporting artifact is associated with the detailed exit interview format?
choices: A full transcript of every fieldwork meeting.
A complete record of server configuration changes.
A full summary of employee attendance during the audit period.
A brief preliminary position paper with the top metrics.
questions.explanation: The exit interview is supported by an executive summary slide deck or a brief preliminary position paper detailing top-level metrics.

questions.question: Which quality of a good data analysis means the methodology could produce the same conclusions when repeated?
choices: Reproducible results.
Outcome-oriented.
Context-aware.
Accurate and defensible.
questions.explanation: Reproducible means the methodology is clear enough that another security professional could analyze the same raw data and reach the same conclusions.

questions.question: Which quality of a good exit interview keeps every statement grounded in verifiable logs or screenshots?
choices: Transparent and clear.
Interactive and open dialogue.
Objective and evidence based.
Constructive and forward looking.
questions.explanation: Objective and evidence-based means every statement is grounded in verifiable logs, screenshots, or configuration files, never assumptions or personal opinions.

questions.question: In the detailed exit interview structure, how are preliminary findings and risks categorized?
choices: By the order in which they were discovered.
By threat levels like Critical, High, and Medium.
By the number of systems that were affected.
By the department responsible for every control area.
questions.explanation: Preliminary risk and finding highlights give an overview of key vulnerabilities categorized by high-level threat levels such as Critical, High, and Medium.

questions.question: Which purpose of data analysis evaluates findings based on likelihood versus impact?
choices: Compliance verification.
Root cause identification.
False positive elimination review.
Risk and resource prioritization.
questions.explanation: Risk prioritization evaluates findings based on likelihood versus impact to determine where remediation resources should be allocated first.

questions.question: Which list of baseline standards is cited in the reference for verifying compliance during data analysis?
choices: ISO 27001, NIST, and PCI-DSS.
COBIT, TOGAF, and ITIL frameworks.
GDPR, HIPAA, and SOX.
FIPS, OSI, and IEEE.
questions.explanation: The reference gives ISO 27001, NIST, and PCI-DSS as examples of baseline security standards and legal frameworks used to validate technical configurations.

questions.question: Which severity scoring framework does the reference cite for objective vulnerability assessment?
choices: OWASP Top 10.
The CVSS framework.
CVE database.
SANS Critical Controls.
questions.explanation: The reference cites CVSS as a standardized scoring framework used to evaluate vulnerability severity objectively.

questions.question: In an audit finding, which component describes what was found or observed?
choices: Criteria.
Cause.
Condition.
The effect.
questions.explanation: Condition describes what was found or observed, while criteria states what should have been in place, cause explains why the issue occurred, and effect or risk covers the possible impact.

questions.question: Which quality of a good audit report is reflected by issuing the report promptly?
choices: Confidential.
Objective.
Constructive.
Timeliness.
questions.explanation: Timely means the report is issued promptly, one of the six qualities of a good audit report along with accurate, objective, clear, constructive, and confidential.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of presenting audit findings?
choices: Immediate clarity and direct dialogue.
Faster writing of the final audit report.
Reduced need for audit evidence.
Elimination of follow-up audits.
questions.explanation: Presenting findings gives immediate clarity and direct dialogue, letting stakeholders ask questions and eliminating misunderstandings before final reports are archived.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of presenting audit findings?
choices: It delays stakeholder acceptance.
It removes important technical detail.
It can oversimplify and cause misuse.
It prevents discussion of matters in scope.
questions.explanation: Condensing detailed technical or financial data into summary slides can lead to oversimplification or takeaways taken out of context.

questions.question: In the IT example, what audit finding was presented?
choices: Outdated printer firmware was found in the office.
Workstations missed critical patches and credentials.
The help desk ticket backlog far exceeded expectations.
Email encryption was disabled for executives.
questions.explanation: The example finding was that 58% of workstations were missing critical security patches and default administrator credentials were active on network switches.

questions.question: What risk did the Cold Room B finding highlight in the quality and safety example?
choices: Loss of customer orders.
Higher energy and utility bills.
Damaged packaging.
Regulatory non-compliance.
questions.explanation: The Cold Room B finding, where temperatures exceeded the 4C limit, highlighted regulatory non-compliance risks and led to a proposed automated IoT temperature-alerting framework.

questions.question: Which chain correctly summarizes how an audit report is produced?
choices: Evidence, analysis, findings, opinion, report.
Opinion, findings, analysis, evidence, report.
Findings, evidence, opinion, analysis, report.
Analysis, opinion, evidence, findings, report.
questions.explanation: The reference summarizes the flow as Audit Evidence, Analysis, Findings, Opinion or Conclusion, then the Audit Report.

chapters.title: Log Information and Security Controls
chapters.description: Covers security logging, types of log information, the Intrusion Detection System (IDS), detection and profiling methods, the host-based IDS, layered defense, Network Access Control, host isolation, system hardening, and monitoring and testing security controls.

questions.question: What do security logs record?
choices: Approved financial transactions recorded by senior management.
The physical location of every employee each working day.
Activity on computers, networks, applications, and devices.
Only the successful logins on a single host system.
questions.explanation: Security logs record activities occurring on computers, networks, applications, and security devices.

questions.question: Which is listed as something security logs help organizations do?
choices: Verify security controls and detect access attempts.
Replace security monitoring tools in the enterprise.
Auto-generate user credentials for all employees.
Assign network permissions directly to each user.
questions.explanation: Logs help organizations detect unauthorized access, investigate incidents, verify security controls, and support audits and compliance.

questions.question: Which set of questions does the reference list as important for logs?
choices: Why, how, how much, and how often.
Who, why, which tool, and which vendor.
What, why, how, and how much.
Who, what, when, and where it happened.
questions.explanation: The important log questions are who performed the action, what happened, when it happened, and where it originated.

questions.question: Which event belongs under authentication logs?
choices: Access to a restricted company file.
A multi-factor authentication event.
A firewall connection is being blocked.
An operating-system error event.
questions.explanation: Authentication logs capture successful and failed logins, password changes, multi-factor authentication events, and account lockouts.

questions.question: Which event belongs under authorization logs?
choices: A failed login attempt event.
A software installation event.
An administrative action.
A VPN connection event.
questions.explanation: Authorization logs cover access to restricted files, privilege changes, and administrative actions.

questions.question: Which event belongs under network logs?
choices: A password change.
A network scan event.
A configuration change.
An application failure.
questions.explanation: Network logs capture firewall connections, blocked traffic, VPN activity, and network scans.

questions.question: Which event belongs under system and application logs?
choices: Software installations.
Account lockouts.
Blocked traffic flow.
Privilege change events.
questions.explanation: System and application logs cover operating-system errors, software installations, configuration changes, and application failures.

questions.question: Which set does NIST identify as important information for IDPS events?
choices: Alert ID number, vendor name, and sensor model type.
Username, department, and manager details.
Packet size, port number, and payload data.
Timestamp, event type, source, reporting system.
questions.explanation: NIST identifies the timestamp, event type, event source, and sensor or reporting system as important information for IDPS events.

questions.question: How does an IDS generally respond to detected activity?
choices: It blocks the network activity automatically.
It generates alerts instead of blocking it.
It quarantines the entire network segment.
It resets all affected user accounts.
questions.explanation: An IDS generally generates alerts rather than blocking activity automatically.

questions.question: Which of these can an IDS monitor?
choices: Employee salary records.
Vendor service contracts.
Authentication attempts.
Physical access cards.
questions.explanation: An IDS can monitor network traffic, system activity, user behavior, application events, and authentication attempts.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes NIDS from HIDS?
choices: NIDS scans network traffic; HIDS scans individual hosts.
HIDS monitors network traffic; NIDS monitors network servers.
NIDS only generates alerts; HIDS only blocks.
HIDS requires a SIEM platform; NIDS does not.
questions.explanation: A network-based IDS (NIDS) monitors network traffic, while a host-based IDS (HIDS) monitors individual computers or servers.

questions.question: Which item appears in IDS log information per the reference?
choices: Processor temperature reading.
Employee badge number.
Router serial number.
Detection rule or signature.
questions.explanation: IDS log information includes the alert identification number, date and time, source and destination IPs, ports and protocol, detection rule or signature, attack type, severity, affected host, sensor, and response taken.

questions.question: Which detection method combines multiple events to reveal a larger attack?
choices: Protocol analysis.
Event correlation.
Signature-based detection.
Anomaly-based detection.
questions.explanation: Event correlation combines multiple events to identify a larger attack.

questions.question: Which action is part of verifying that security controls work as intended?
choices: Confirm that logging is enabled on key devices.
Disable logging on nonessential devices.
Remove timestamps from important system log entries.
Approve the final audit report drafts.
questions.explanation: Verification includes reviewing configurations, confirming logging is enabled, performing an authorized test intrusion, confirming the alert, and validating timestamps.

questions.question: Where should security control testing be performed, per the reference?
choices: On live production systems without notice.
In the vendor's data center only.
During the annual report review.
In an authorized, controlled environment.
questions.explanation: Security control testing should be authorized and performed in a controlled environment.

questions.question: Which practice is recommended for protecting logs?
choices: Storing logs only on the systems that generate them.
Giving all administrators edit access to logs.
Storing logs in a centralized platform or SIEM.
Deleting logs after every incident.
questions.explanation: Logs should be stored in a centralized log-management platform or SIEM and separated from the systems generating them.

questions.question: How should logs be protected during transmission and storage?
choices: By encryption.
By compression.
By duplication.
By isolation.
questions.explanation: Logs should be encrypted during transmission and storage.

questions.question: Why should log storage be separated from the systems generating the logs?
choices: To reduce the overall cost of storage hardware.
To speed up log file writing speed.
To simplify software licensing terms.
To keep logs safe if a system is compromised.
questions.explanation: Separate log storage keeps the logs safe if the systems that generate them are compromised, and helps monitor attempts to modify or delete them.

questions.question: Which technique is recommended to protect the integrity of logs?
choices: Renaming log files on a schedule.
Using hashes or append-only storage.
Compressing logs into storage archives.
Rotating log file locations.
questions.explanation: Hashes, digital signatures, or append-only storage are used to protect log integrity.

questions.question: Which function is part of log management per the reference?
choices: Authorizing user accounts.
Scheduling routine software updates.
Disposing of log data properly.
Assigning file permissions.
questions.explanation: Log management includes generating, transmitting, storing, accessing, and disposing of log data.

questions.question: Which item should security teams investigate during log review?
choices: Daily printer maintenance records.
Weekly meeting room bookings.
Quarterly software license counts.
Unexpected administrator activity.
questions.explanation: Teams should investigate repeated failed logins, privilege escalation, disabled security services, malware detection, unexpected administrator activity, and large or unusual data transfers.

questions.question: When suspicious activity is identified, what is the first action in the listed sequence?
choices: Validate the alert.
Contain the activity.
Preserve evidence.
Improve security controls.
questions.explanation: The sequence starts by validating the alert, then identifying affected systems, preserving evidence, containing, investigating and documenting, and finally improving controls.

questions.question: Signature-based analysis is also known as what?
choices: Specification-based detection.
Anomaly detection.
Misuse-based detection.
Stateful analysis.
questions.explanation: Signature-based analysis is also known as misuse detection because it scans for signatures that match recorded threats.

questions.question: What does anomaly-based detection flag as a potential attack?
choices: An exact match to a known attack signature.
A deviation from a baseline of normal behavior.
Improper use of a standard network protocol.
A combination of two unrelated random network events.
questions.explanation: Anomaly-based detection builds a baseline profile of standard operations and logs any deviation from it as a potential attack.

questions.question: Stateful protocol analysis is also known as what?
choices: Rule-based detection method.
Misuse-based detection method.
Behavior profiling techniques.
Specification-based analysis.
questions.explanation: Stateful protocol analysis, also called specification-based analysis, compares network activity against vendor profiles of how protocols should structurally behave.

questions.question: What is a documented limitation of signature-based analysis?
choices: Blindness to zero-day vulnerabilities.
A high rate of false positives.
Heavy system resource consumption.
Dependence on vendor protocol profiles.
questions.explanation: Signature-based analysis is entirely blind to new, zero-day vulnerabilities and morphing malware, though it is highly accurate for known threats.

questions.question: What is a documented limitation of anomaly-based analysis?
choices: It cannot detect novel attacks.
It cannot build a proper baseline profile.
It produces a high rate of false positives.
It must track network pairings constantly over time.
questions.explanation: Anomaly-based analysis causes a high rate of false positives from legitimate unusual user spikes or system changes.

questions.question: What is a documented limitation of stateful protocol analysis?
choices: It fails to catch protocol manipulation.
It consumes heavy system resources.
It relies on learned history.
It ignores protocol state changes.
questions.explanation: Stateful protocol analysis consumes heavy system resources because it continuously tracks state conditions across layers.

questions.question: Which supplementary technique alerts defenders when pre-set operational limits are broken?
choices: Threshold monitoring.
Resource profiling.
Executable profiling.
File integrity monitoring.
questions.explanation: Threshold monitoring alerts defenders when pre-set operational limits are broken, such as a limit on failed login attempts.

questions.question: Which supplementary technique tracks CPU, RAM, and bandwidth to find background malware?
choices: Executable profiling.
Threshold monitoring.
Signature matching.
Resource profiling.
questions.explanation: Resource profiling tracks system-wide metrics like CPU, RAM, and bandwidth to find sneaky background malware.

questions.question: Which supplementary technique analyzes how software programs invoke system calls and read memory?
choices: Resource profiling.
Executable profiling.
Threshold monitoring.
Anomaly profiling.
questions.explanation: Executable profiling continuously analyzes how active programs invoke system calls and read system memory.

questions.question: Which activity is part of how a HIDS works?
choices: Controlling exactly which devices join the network.
Encrypting the host's storage volume.
Comparing file states to baseline snapshots.
Blocking all external IP addresses.
questions.explanation: A HIDS performs file integrity monitoring by comparing current states of critical files and configurations against baseline snapshots.

questions.question: Which data does the HIDS agent collect directly from the host?
choices: Kernel activities and system logs.
Network switch configuration files.
Firewall and network rule sets.
Cloud billing and usage summaries.
questions.explanation: The HIDS agent gathers system logs, application event logs, authentication records, and kernel activities directly from the host.

questions.question: What is layered defense, also called defense in depth?
choices: One control repeated at several points in a system.
A policy requiring two approvals per change.
A backup strategy that duplicates one server several times.
Multiple security controls at different system levels.
questions.explanation: Layered defense uses multiple security controls at different levels so that if one layer fails, another can detect, prevent, or limit the attack.

questions.question: Firewalls, segmentation, and NAC are examples in which security layer?
choices: Data security.
Network security.
Application security.
Physical security.
questions.explanation: Network security protects network connections and traffic with firewalls, segmentation, and NAC.

questions.question: What does Network Access Control (NAC) determine?
choices: Which servers need software patch updates.
Which log sources send alert data.
Which users and devices may connect to resources.
Which ports may be opened by various applications.
questions.explanation: NAC controls which users and devices are allowed to connect to and use network resources.

questions.question: Which is a possible NAC decision?
choices: Defer the connection attempt.
Approve the connection attempt fully.
Notify the requester only.
Restrict the connection attempt.
questions.explanation: Possible NAC decisions are allow, deny, restrict, and quarantine.

questions.question: What is the general sequence followed in the NAC process?
choices: Identification, authentication, assessment, authorization, monitoring.
Assessment, identification, monitoring, authorization, authentication.
Authentication, monitoring, identification, assessment, authorization.
Authorization, authentication, assessment, identification, monitoring.
questions.explanation: NAC generally follows identification, authentication, security assessment, authorization, and monitoring.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of host isolation?
choices: Repairing damaged hardware.
Containing the compromised host.
Installing security updates.
Reconfiguring the entire network.
questions.explanation: Host isolation separates a suspected compromised host from other systems, and its primary purpose is containment.

questions.question: Which statement defines system hardening?
choices: Physically securing the server rooms from intruders.
Replacing old hardware with newer server models.
Reducing vulnerabilities via secure configuration.
Backing up data to removable external media.
questions.explanation: System hardening reduces or eliminates vulnerabilities by configuring the operating system, applications, network services, and user accounts according to security best practices.

chapters.title: Risk Management Process
chapters.description: Covers risk identification tools and the risk register, qualitative and quantitative risk assessment, likelihood and impact analysis and the risk matrix, risk response strategies, and implementing and monitoring risk responses.

questions.question: Which statement best describes risk identification?
choices: Evaluating the likelihood and impact of the known risks.
Choosing how to respond to an identified risk.
Finding, recognizing, and documenting potential risks.
Monitoring risks throughout the project's lifecycle.
questions.explanation: Risk identification is the process of finding, recognizing, and documenting potential risks that may affect a project, and it is the starting point of risk management.

questions.question: Risk identification is described as the starting point of what process?
choices: The risk management process.
The audit reporting process.
The data analysis process.
The project closure process.
questions.explanation: Risk identification is the starting point of the risk management process.

questions.question: Which technique has team members name risks such as lack of resources, technical errors, or delays?
choices: Documentation review.
Expert interviews.
SWOT analysis.
Brainstorming.
questions.explanation: Brainstorming lets team members identify risks such as lack of resources, technical errors, or delays.

questions.question: A software project checklist includes risks like security problems, data loss, and system downtime. Which technique does this illustrate?
choices: Historical information.
Checklists of common risks.
SWOT analysis technique.
Expert interviews and sessions.
questions.explanation: Checklists use a list of common risks from previous projects or established standards to identify possible risks.

questions.question: Which technique examines Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats?
choices: Documentation review.
Brainstorming.
Expert interviews.
SWOT analysis.
questions.explanation: SWOT analysis examines strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.

questions.question: Which technique asks people with specialized knowledge about possible risks?
choices: Expert interviews.
Checklists.
Historical information.
Documentation review.
questions.explanation: Expert interviews ask people with specialized knowledge or experience about possible risks.

questions.question: Which technique reviews contracts, schedules, requirements, and reports to find risks?
choices: Brainstorming sessions.
Documentation review.
SWOT analysis method.
Expert interviews.
questions.explanation: Documentation review examines existing project documents, contracts, schedules, requirements, and reports to find potential risks.

questions.question: Which technique examines risks from previous or similar projects?
choices: Checklists of risks.
A full SWOT analysis review.
Historical information.
Brainstorming risks.
questions.explanation: Historical information involves examining risks from previous or similar projects to determine which risks might occur again.

questions.question: What is the main output of the risk identification process?
choices: A risk register.
A risk response plan.
A lessons learned report.
An audit trail.
questions.explanation: The main output of risk identification is a risk register, the document that records the risks identified throughout the project.

questions.question: Which order matches the identification process in the reference?
choices: Document, identify, assess, record.
Assess, identify, record, document.
Record, document, assess, identify.
Identify, document, record, assess.
questions.explanation: The process is identify, document, record in the risk register, then proceed to risk assessment.

questions.question: What does risk assessment help an organization decide?
choices: Which projects to start and fund first.
Which risks need treatment and their order.
Which tools to use for monitoring them.
Which controls to test and report on first.
questions.explanation: Risk assessment determines which risks need treatment and in what order, producing a prioritized understanding of risk exposure.

questions.question: Which risk assessment type uses descriptive ratings like Low, Medium, and High?
choices: Quantitative.
Statistical.
Qualitative.
Analytical.
questions.explanation: Qualitative risk assessment uses descriptive, judgment-based ratings like Low, Medium, or High.

questions.question: Which risk assessment type uses dollar amounts and probabilities?
choices: Qualitative ratings.
Descriptive in nature.
Comparative ratings.
Quantitative values.
questions.explanation: Quantitative risk assessment uses numerical, data-driven values such as dollar amounts and probabilities.

questions.question: Which pair of examples matches qualitative and quantitative assessment in the reference?
choices: A Medium rating for a vendor, then a 2.3M annual loss.
A 2.3M loss estimate, then a High inspector rating.
A probability score, then a descriptive risk matrix tool.
A CVSS score, then a likelihood rating value.
questions.explanation: The startup's quick Medium vendor rating illustrates qualitative assessment, while the bank's expected annual loss calculation illustrates quantitative assessment.

questions.question: What does likelihood represent in risk analysis?
choices: The severity of consequences if a risk occurs.
The probability that a risk event will occur.
The cost of treating a risk.
The time needed to recover from a risk.
questions.explanation: Likelihood is the probability that a risk event will occur.

questions.question: What does impact represent in risk analysis?
choices: The probability the risk event will occur.
The total number of risks identified.
The severity of consequences if it occurs.
The budget assigned to treat the risk.
questions.explanation: Impact is the severity of consequences if the risk event occurs.

questions.question: How is overall risk level calculated in the reference?
choices: The likelihood plus the impact.
The impact divided by the likelihood.
The likelihood minus the impact.
The likelihood times the impact.
questions.explanation: Risk Level equals Likelihood multiplied by Impact.

questions.question: In the risk matrix, which axis represents likelihood?
choices: The Y-axis.
The X-axis.
Both axes.
Neither axis.
questions.explanation: The risk matrix plots likelihood on the Y-axis and impact on the X-axis.

questions.question: How should high-severity risks be treated after ranking?
choices: Monitored or accepted by the senior management team.
Addressed with immediate mitigation or action.
Transferred to the insurance provider firm.
Deferred to the next review cycle.
questions.explanation: High-severity risks call for immediate mitigation or action, while low-severity risks are monitored or accepted.

questions.question: Which risk response strategy eliminates the risk entirely?
choices: Mitigate the risk impact.
Transfer the whole risk.
Avoid the risk entirely.
Accept the risk as is.
questions.explanation: Avoid means eliminating the risk entirely.

questions.question: Which risk response strategy reduces the likelihood or impact of a risk?
choices: Avoid.
Accept.
Transfer.
Mitigate.
questions.explanation: Mitigate reduces the likelihood or impact of a risk.

questions.question: Which risk response strategy shifts the risk to a third party?
choices: Transfer.
Avoid.
Mitigate.
Accept.
questions.explanation: Transfer shifts the risk to a third party, such as through insurance.

questions.question: Which risk response strategy acknowledges the risk and monitors it without taking action?
choices: Transfer.
Accept.
Mitigate.
Avoid.
questions.explanation: Accept means acknowledging the risk and monitoring it without action.

questions.question: Which element is required for a successful risk response implementation?
choices: A single decision-making leader.
Minimal documentation kept.
Open dialogue with stakeholders.
A private budget for the team.
questions.explanation: Successful implementation requires clear ownership, adequate resources, and open communication with stakeholders at every stage.

questions.question: Which tool is listed for monitoring and controlling risk responses?
choices: Automated vulnerability scanners.
Key Risk Indicators and dashboards.
Automated network mapping software.
Scheduled backup restoration drills.
questions.explanation: Monitoring techniques and tools include regular risk audits, Key Risk Indicators and dashboards, status reports and team check-ins, and stakeholder feedback loops.

chapters.title: Business Continuity Management
chapters.description: Covers foundational continuity definitions, recovery metrics (RTO, RPO, MTD, WRT, MBCO), Maximum Tolerable Downtime, the Business Impact Analysis, plan review, and testing the plan.

questions.question: Which statement defines Business Continuity Management (BCM)?
choices: A framework of policies and processes for handling disruptive incidents.
A documented set of procedures followed only during a single disruption.
A technical plan for restoring all servers after an outage.
A financial reserve maintained for unexpected business expenses.
questions.explanation: BCM is an organization-wide framework of policies, processes, and capabilities that prepare a business to prevent, respond to, and recover from disruptive incidents.

questions.question: Which statement defines a Business Continuity Plan (BCP)?
choices: A broad framework of policies for managing the daily business operations.
Procedures for keeping critical functions running during a disruption.
A technical plan for restoring data after a system failure.
A yearly schedule for reviewing the continuity program.
questions.explanation: A BCP is the documented set of procedures an organization follows to keep critical functions running during, and immediately after, a disruption.

questions.question: Which statement defines Disaster Recovery (DR)?
choices: An organization-wide continuity management framework.
A set of procedures for keeping critical functions running during a disruption.
A technical, IT-focused effort to restore systems and data after an outage.
A policy governing employee emergency responses during incidents.
questions.explanation: Disaster Recovery is a technical, IT-focused subset of continuity planning concerned with restoring systems, data, and infrastructure after an outage.

questions.question: What does the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) measure?
choices: The maximum acceptable amount of data lost.
The time needed to verify restored data sets.
The absolute limit of disruption before survival is threatened.
The maximum acceptable time to restore a business function.
questions.explanation: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore a business function after a disruption occurs.

questions.question: What does the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) define?
choices: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss as a point in time.
The time needed to resume normal processing after the restoration.
The maximum downtime the business can tolerate or survive.
The minimum service level to be maintained during a disruption.
questions.explanation: RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as the point in time to which data must be restored.

questions.question: What does Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) represent?
choices: The preferred recovery target for restoring services.
The absolute limit of disruption an organization can survive.
The average downtime measured across all past recorded outages.
The budget assigned for continuity investments.
questions.explanation: MTD is the absolute limit of disruption a function can withstand before survival of the business is threatened.

questions.question: What does Work Recovery Time (WRT) cover?
choices: The time needed to restore systems after an outage.
Time lost while waiting for vendor support teams.
Time after restoration to verify data and resume processing.
The time between detection and the formal first notification.
questions.explanation: WRT is the time needed after systems are restored to verify data and resume normal processing.

questions.question: How does the reference order incident, crisis, and disaster?
choices: By the total amount of media coverage received.
By the number of departments involved.
By the duration of the response effort.
By escalating levels of severity and impact.
questions.explanation: Incident, crisis, and disaster are escalating levels of severity: an incident is minor, a crisis threatens objectives and reputation, and a disaster causes major, prolonged damage.

questions.question: Which statement describes resilience?
choices: The ability to absorb and adapt without losing required function.
The capacity to restore lost data from available backup storage sets.
The speed and uptime of the network connection.
The number of backup sites that remain available.
questions.explanation: Resilience is the ability to absorb and adapt to disruption without losing function.

questions.question: What is a single point of failure (SPOF)?
choices: A device that fails during periods of peak system load.
A component whose failure stops the entire process.
A server that has no backup at all.
A process that depends on one external vendor.
questions.explanation: A SPOF is any single component whose failure stops the entire process.

questions.question: What does continuity of operations emphasize?
choices: Eventual restoration of services only after the whole disruption.
Reducing the overall cost caused by disruptions.
Sustained delivery of critical services during a disruption.
Timely notification of all the relevant stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Continuity of operations is the sustained delivery of critical services and functions throughout a disruption, not merely their eventual restoration.

questions.question: Why is MTD described as a boundary rather than a recovery target?
choices: It is the average downtime across incidents.
It is adjusted automatically after every continuity test.
It is optional for all non-critical business functions.
It is the outer boundary that recovery must stay within.
questions.explanation: MTD is not a target to aim for; it is the outer boundary every recovery strategy must stay inside before consequences become unacceptable.

questions.question: Which factor drives Maximum Tolerable Downtime, per the reference?
choices: Financial impact from lost revenue and penalties.
The number of backup locations available.
The size of the continuity team in place.
The type of operating system currently being deployed.
questions.explanation: MTD is driven by financial impact, reputational damage, regulatory and legal obligations, and operational dependencies.

questions.question: Why must MTD differ by business function, according to the reference?
choices: Because different functions use different software.
Because some functions tolerate more downtime than others.
Because each function is given a separate budget.
Because every function reports to completely different executives.
questions.explanation: MTD differs by function; for example, payroll tolerates more downtime than trading.

questions.question: How does the cost of downtime behave as time passes?
choices: It stays completely constant until the MTD is reached.
It declines as buffers absorb the impact.
It accelerates and compounds the impact over time.
It resets after each recovery milestone.
questions.explanation: Impact rarely rises in a straight line; it accelerates, with each additional day compounding financial, legal, and reputational cost.

questions.question: How do RPO, RTO, and WRT relate to the MTD?
choices: They each set separate recovery limits unrelated to MTD.
They are measured after normal operations resume.
They replace the need for an MTD entirely.
Their combined values must stay inside the MTD boundary.
questions.explanation: Together, RPO plus RTO plus WRT must fit comfortably inside the MTD boundary.

questions.question: Which is the first step to determine acceptable downtime?
choices: Identify the critical processes that cannot be interrupted.
Derive the RTO and the RPO targets from the recovery ceiling.
Set the MTD threshold based on the impact analysis.
Model the cumulative impact over multiple time periods.
questions.explanation: The first step is to identify the critical processes, the functions the organization cannot operate without.

questions.question: Which is the final step in determining acceptable downtime?
choices: Consult stakeholders, regulators, and auditors.
Derive RTO and RPO targets inside the ceiling.
Quantify the financial impact over time.
Identify the critical processes first.
questions.explanation: After setting the MTD threshold, the final step is working backward to set RTO and RPO targets safely inside that ceiling.

questions.question: Which statement defines a Business Impact Analysis (BIA)?
choices: A consistent method for ranking project risks by their likelihood.
A financial audit of all recovery investments.
A process to identify and evaluate the effects of a disruption.
A review of the continuity plan's version history.
questions.explanation: A BIA is a process to identify and evaluate the effects of a disruption to critical business operations.

questions.question: Which comparison distinguishes a BIA from a risk assessment?
choices: BIA asks what could go wrong; risk assessment asks the required recovery speed.
Both answer the same continuity question in different terms.
Risk assessment measures the impact; BIA measures the likelihood.
BIA asks the impact and recovery speed; risk assessment asks what can go wrong.
questions.explanation: Risk assessment asks what could go wrong, while BIA asks what the impact is and how quickly recovery must happen.

questions.question: Which metric sets the minimum service level the business must maintain during a disruption?
choices: Minimum Business Continuity Objective (MBCO).
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) time target.
Work Recovery Time (WRT) time target.
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) time data target.
questions.explanation: The Minimum Business Continuity Objective (MBCO) is the minimum service level the business must maintain during a disruption.

questions.question: Which impact type covers SLA breaches, penalties, and contract termination?
choices: Reputational.
Contractual.
Operational.
Strategic.
questions.explanation: Contractual impact covers SLA breaches, penalties, and contract termination.

questions.question: How many increasing time intervals does the BIA process use to assess impact?
choices: Three.
Four.
Five.
Seven.
questions.explanation: The BIA steps assess impact at seven increasing time intervals across the impact categories.

questions.question: Which tool is listed for carrying out a BIA?
choices: Structured interviews and workshops.
Automated network vulnerability scans.
Weekly server backup logs.
Quarterly firewall rule reviews.
questions.explanation: Common BIA tools include structured interviews and workshops, questionnaires or surveys, dependency mapping, impact-over-time analysis, criticality ranking matrices, and BCM software.

questions.question: Why must a continuity plan be regularly reviewed?
choices: Because live testing is too expensive.
Because regulators require regular formal annual updates.
Because plans drift out of step as conditions change.
Because the plan is written only once.
questions.explanation: A continuity plan is only accurate the day it is written; people, systems, and risks change, so the plan must be reviewed to stay current.

questions.question: Which event should trigger a plan review, per the reference?
choices: A change in the weather forecast pattern.
A merger or organizational restructure.
A quarterly departmental marketing report.
A routine staff training session.
questions.explanation: Reviews are triggered by scheduled intervals, organizational or technology changes such as restructures and mergers, and after an incident or audit finding.

questions.question: Who provides independent assurance that the plan review was thorough and objective?
choices: Senior management.
The BC manager.
Internal audit.
Department heads.
questions.explanation: Internal audit provides independent assurance that the review was thorough and objective.

questions.question: Which reason explains why continuity plans should be tested?
choices: To identify and assign new emergency contacts.
To validate assumptions and uncover gaps before an event.
To approve and confirm the annual continuity budget items.
To update the BIA questionnaires and forms.
questions.explanation: Testing validates assumptions, uncovers missing steps or outdated contacts, trains staff, and satisfies compliance.

questions.question: Which step completes the testing cycle described in the reference?
choices: Plan the testing and exercise approach first.
Test the current continuity plan.
Review the test results and findings.
Update the plan with the lessons learned.
questions.explanation: The testing cycle is Plan, Test, Review results, then Update the plan by folding lessons learned back into it.

questions.question: Which key takeaway states that every recovery target must remain beneath the MTD?
choices: MTD is the ceiling each recovery target must fit beneath.
RTO is the ceiling that each recovery target must exceed.
RPO determines the budget set for recovery.
WRT replaces the MTD notion in testing.
questions.explanation: A core takeaway is that Maximum Tolerable Downtime is the ceiling every recovery target (RTO, RPO, WRT) must fit beneath.

chapters.title: Backing Up Data and Application
chapters.description: Covers backup types, the preparation, identification, and three-phase response model (notification, response, recovery), post-incident review, documentation, and reporting including data privacy law requirements.

questions.question: Which statement best defines backing up data?
choices: Creating copies of files so the originals can be restored if damaged.
Moving old files between network drives to free up extra storage space.
Deleting outdated files to reduce the storage footprint.
Encrypting files so only authorized users can read them.
questions.explanation: Backing up data means creating copies of files and systems so they can be restored if the originals are lost, damaged, or corrupted.

questions.question: Which statement matches a full backup?
choices: Fastest to create and uses the least storage.
Slowest to create, fastest to restore, uses most storage.
Copies only data changed since the last backup.
Creates a continuously updated copy with no version history.
questions.explanation: A full backup is the slowest to create and the fastest to restore, and it uses the most storage.

questions.question: Which statement matches an incremental backup?
choices: Copies all the changes since the last full backup.
Creates a real-time copy with no versions.
Copies only data changed since the last backup.
Restores quickly using only one backup set.
questions.explanation: An incremental backup copies only data that has changed since the last backup, whether full or incremental, and is faster and more storage-efficient.

questions.question: Which statement matches a differential backup?
choices: Copies only data changed since the last backup of any kind.
Creates a continuously updated real-time copy.
Restores slowly because many sets are required.
Copies all data changed since the last full backup.
questions.explanation: A differential backup copies all data changed since the last full backup, so restoring requires only the full backup and the latest differential.

questions.question: Which risk is associated with a mirror backup?
choices: A deleted source file is also removed from the mirror copy.
Restore generally takes longer than with incremental backups.
Storage use grows faster than with differentials.
It cannot be restored after a device failure.
questions.explanation: A mirror backup does not keep older versions; if a file is deleted from the source, it is also removed from the mirror.

questions.question: Why is a differential backup faster to restore than an incremental one?
choices: It uses less storage space overall.
Only the full and the latest differential are needed.
It copies less data every single day.
It is stored on a separate backup medium every single night.
questions.explanation: A differential restore needs only two sets, the full backup and the latest differential, while incremental restores may require many sets.

questions.question: What is the goal of the Preparation phase in incident handling?
choices: To confirm that an actual security incident has occurred.
To notify law enforcement authorities.
To get the organization ready for a possible incident.
To restore systems from verified backups.
questions.explanation: Preparation is the first phase of incident handling, and its goal is to get the organization ready before an incident happens.

questions.question: Which item is part of the Policies and Plans preparation step?
choices: Preparing a forensic jump kit and tools.
Deploying antivirus and EDR software.
Running simulated incident response drills.
Defining Incident Response Team roles.
questions.explanation: Policies and Plans includes establishing an incident response policy, developing an IRP, defining roles such as the Incident Response Team, and setting communication and escalation procedures.

questions.question: Which item belongs to the Tools and Resources preparation step?
choices: Maintaining an updated inventory of hardware and software.
Developing an escalation procedure and plan.
Conducting the employee security awareness training sessions.
Writing the incident response policy document.
questions.explanation: Tools and Resources includes deploying security tools, maintaining an updated inventory, preparing a forensic jump kit, and ensuring backup systems are in place and tested.

questions.question: What does the Identification stage accomplish?
choices: It restores the affected systems from verified clean backups.
It separates true incidents from false alarms and sets scope.
It assigns owners to the corrective actions.
It eradicates all malware from the affected hosts.
questions.explanation: Identification detects and confirms that an incident occurred, determines scope, nature, and severity, and separates true incidents from false alarms.

questions.question: Which source can indicate a security incident, per the reference?
choices: Employee payroll records.
Vendor purchase orders.
Alerts from IDS, IPS, and SIEM.
Employee vacation and leave schedules.
questions.explanation: Signs of an incident can come from IDS, IPS, antivirus, and SIEM alerts, log analysis, employee reports, and performance anomalies.

questions.question: What is included in the verification steps of Identification?
choices: Containing the affected systems quickly first.
Deploying short-term containment fixes.
Eradicating the underlying root cause.
Documenting findings for chain of custody.
questions.explanation: Verification includes confirming the event is real, gathering initial evidence, classifying the incident type and severity, and documenting findings as discovered for chain of custody.

questions.question: What are the three phases of the response model in the reference?
choices: The phases of notification, response, and recovery.
Phases of detection, containment, and eradication.
Phases of preparation, identification, and recovery.
Phases of containment, eradication, and restoration.
questions.explanation: The three-phase response model is Notification, Response, and Recovery.

questions.question: Why should notification lists be prepared before an incident occurs?
choices: To reduce the total number of final notifications.
So the right people are reached the first time during a crisis.
To keep the incident response team small, focused, and effective.
To satisfy insurance policy requirements.
questions.explanation: Notification lists should be prepared before an incident so teams do not write them from scratch during one; defined communication chains help reach the right people first time.

questions.question: Which group is included in a notification list to assess regulatory obligations?
choices: Affected users and customers.
Internal IT and security teams.
Legal and compliance officers.
Network administrators.
questions.explanation: Legal and compliance officers assess regulatory obligations, liability exposure, and mandatory disclosure requirements.

questions.question: How does timely notification help an organization, per the reference?
choices: It increases the total recovery budget available.
It replaces the need for complete containment steps entirely.
It prevents all future incidents from occurring.
It limits the damage before the security threat spreads.
questions.explanation: Timely notification limits damage by letting security teams isolate the threat early, meets legal deadlines, preserves trust, and speeds recovery.

questions.question: How should incident reports be kept as new information emerges?
choices: Strictly factual and updated.
Speculative to prompt discussion.
Brief and finalized early.
Shared only after investigation ends.
questions.explanation: Incident reports must be strictly factual and updated as new information emerges, avoiding speculation.

questions.question: Which action belongs to containing an incident?
choices: Restoring all critical data from the verified backups.
Disconnecting compromised devices to stop movement.
Reviewing the lessons learned after an incident.
Drafting the final breach report for management.
questions.explanation: Containment includes isolating affected systems, disabling compromised accounts, applying short-term fixes, and preserving evidence.

questions.question: Which action is a short-term containment fix, per the reference?
choices: Rebuilding the compromised host system entirely.
Updating the incident response plan promptly.
Blocking malicious IPs and closing open ports.
Conducting a full security scan.
questions.explanation: Short-term fixes include blocking malicious IPs, closing exploited ports, and applying emergency firewall rules.

questions.question: Which activity is part of removing the cause of an incident?
choices: Performing a gradual system rollout.
Sending stakeholder notifications first.
Continuing proactive security monitoring now.
Removing backdoors and unauthorized accounts.
questions.explanation: Removing the cause covers root cause identification, malware eradication including backdoors and unauthorized accounts, closing the vulnerability, and eradication verification.

questions.question: What is a clean restore point?
choices: A backup taken before the incident and free of malware.
The most recent backup that is available.
A backup created after the eradication.
The very first full backup made during initial system setup.
questions.explanation: Recovery uses a clean restore point, a backup taken before the incident and confirmed free of malware or tampering.

questions.question: How should systems be restored after an incident?
choices: In the order the systems were attacked first.
In priority order based on the recovery priorities.
All affected systems at the same exact time.
From the newest to the oldest backup copy available.
questions.explanation: Systems are restored in priority order, bringing critical business systems back first according to the organization's recovery priorities.

questions.question: Which step verifies that restored systems work properly before going live?
choices: Obtaining legal approval before going live.
Deleting all old logs afterward.
Renewing all software licenses.
Running scans to check for any threats.
questions.explanation: Testing after restore includes verifying functionality, running security scans to confirm no trace of the threat remains, checking performance, and obtaining sign-off.

questions.question: Which method is suggested for finding the real cause instead of the symptom?
choices: Repeating why until you find something fixable.
Reviewing the written backup policy one more time.
Asking who is responsible for it first.
Skipping the initial symptom analysis.
questions.explanation: The 5 Whys method keeps asking why until you reach something you can actually fix, moving past the symptom.

questions.question: Which two questions judge whether a backup really worked?
choices: Who made it and where it was stored.
How big it was and how fast it copied.
How much data was lost and how long it was down.
Which vendor produced the backup and its warranty period.
questions.explanation: A backup is judged by how much data was lost, which relates to the RPO, and how long the organization was down, which relates to the RTO.

questions.question: What should every finding from a post-incident review have?
choices: A budget estimate and vendor name.
A person in charge and a due date.
An approved workaround.
A timeline for annual review.
questions.explanation: Every finding needs a person in charge and a due date, then the response plan, backup policy, and guides are updated.

questions.question: When does incident documentation start, per the reference?
choices: After the incident is contained.
When the report is requested.
The moment the incident is detected.
During the final lessons learned meeting.
questions.explanation: Documentation starts the moment the incident is detected; it is a running log, not something written at the end.

questions.question: How should the incident log be written?
choices: As a running log of each step with the time taken.
As a summary written after everything is fully resolved.
As a separate report for each department.
As a record of the final findings only.
questions.explanation: Responders write each step with the time while still working on the problem, recording facts only and never guesses.

questions.question: Which statement matches how the incident report is tailored for management?
choices: The official breach notice filed before the legal deadline.
Plain-language guidance written for affected users.
A full technical timeline with root cause and all pending fixes.
A short one to two page summary of cost, downtime, and impact.
questions.explanation: Management receives a short 1 to 2 page summary covering cost, downtime, business impact, and what the team needs to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: When does the 72-hour window for notifying the National Privacy Commission begin?
choices: When the entire investigation is fully and entirely finished.
When the incident report is drafted.
When you know or have reason to believe a breach happened.
When all affected users have been fully contacted.
questions.explanation: Under RA 10173 and NPC Circular 16-03, the 72-hour clock starts when you know or have good reason to believe a breach happened, not when the investigation is finished.

encyclopedia.definition: Activities performed after the audit has been conducted to review, analyze, document, and communicate the results of the audit. They help the organization understand the findings, address issues, and determine actions for improvement.

A meeting held at the conclusion of audit fieldwork, when necessary, to discuss audit findings, resolve questions or concerns, and address outstanding issues before the final audit report is released.
The active phase of the audit where evidence is gathered and tests are performed before the exit interview, management responses, draft report review, and final report.
Comments and context that management is allowed to provide after the exit interview, before the final audit report is issued.
The intelligence generated from reviewing audit-related information, often using technology, to find actionable audit insights.
The cleansing step in data analysis that makes data usable by searching for outliers, dealing with null values, and looking for data that may have been incorrectly input.
Analysis that uses data to search for the cause of, and a solution to, an existing problem.
Analysis that describes the data by summarizing key sections.
Analysis that combines historical data and statistical modeling to forecast how certain metrics will perform in the future.
A formal written document that summarizes the results of the audit, communicates the auditor's conclusion or opinion, and identifies risks and areas requiring improvement.
The title that an audit report should mention at the top of the document.
The most critical content in an audit report; it states the impression derived after auditing the financial statements, expressing whether they are free of fraud or error.
The section of the audit report that explains the evidence and procedures supporting the auditor's opinion.

Parts of a finding: Condition (what was found or observed), Criteria (what should have been in place), Cause (why the issue occurred), Effect or Risk (possible impact), and Recommendation (action needed).
The stage where the audit team formally communicates and discusses the results of the audit with relevant stakeholders once the report is finalized or nearing finalization.
A standardized scoring framework applied during data analysis to evaluate the severity of vulnerabilities objectively.

encyclopedia.term: Qualities of a good audit report
encyclopedia.definition: The report should be accurate (evidence-based), objective (free from bias), clear, constructive (practical solutions), timely (issued promptly), and confidential (sensitive information protected).

A record of activities occurring on computers, networks, applications, and security devices, used to detect unauthorized access, investigate incidents, verify controls, and support audits and compliance.
A log covering successful and failed logins, password changes, multi-factor authentication events, and account lockouts.
A log covering access to restricted files, privilege changes, and administrative actions.
A log covering firewall connections, blocked traffic, VPN activity, and network scans.
A log covering operating-system errors, software installations, configuration changes, and application failures and user transactions.
The National Institute of Standards and Technology, which identifies the timestamp, event type, event source, and sensor or reporting system as important information for IDPS events.
A system that monitors activity and detects possible attacks or policy violations; it generally generates alerts rather than blocking activity automatically.
A type of IDS that monitors network traffic.
A type of IDS that monitors individual computers or servers, gathering system logs, application event logs, authentication records, and kernel activities.
Also called misuse detection; matches data against known threat indicators and is highly accurate for known threats but blind to new zero-day vulnerabilities.
Detection that builds a baseline of normal behavior using machine learning or statistics and flags deviations as potential attacks; it detects novel threats but causes many false positives.
Also called specification-based analysis; compares network activity against vendor profiles of how protocols should behave and tracks the state of network pairings over time.
A detection method that combines multiple events to identify a larger attack.
A supplementary profiling technique that alerts defenders when pre-set operational limits, such as failed login attempts, are broken.
A technique that tracks system-wide consumption metrics like CPU, RAM, and bandwidth to find hidden background malware.
A technique that continuously analyzes how active software programs invoke system calls and read system memory.
A HIDS capability that tracks critical files, configuration settings, and executables by comparing current states against baseline snapshots to catch unauthorized changes.
A security strategy that uses multiple security controls at different levels of an information system so that if one layer fails, another can detect, prevent, or limit the attack.
A security approach that controls which users and devices are allowed to connect to and use network resources; it evaluates user identity, device identity, security posture, and network requirements.
A technique that separates a suspected compromised computer, server, or endpoint from other systems, with containment as its primary purpose.
The process of reducing or eliminating vulnerabilities by configuring the operating system, applications, network services, and user accounts according to security best practices.
A centralized log-management platform where logs are stored for protection and analysis.
A security testing method that searches systems for known weaknesses and identifies outdated software and insecure configurations.
A security testing method that simulates controlled attacks against a system to determine whether vulnerabilities can actually be exploited.
The process of finding, recognizing, and documenting potential risks that may affect a project; it is the starting point of the risk management process.
The document that records the risks identified throughout the project; it is the main output of risk identification.
A risk identification technique that examines Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats.
The process of identifying, analyzing, and evaluating risks to determine their significance and decide which risks need treatment and in what order.
Assessment using descriptive, judgment-based ratings like Low, Medium, or High; it is fast, easy to communicate, and relies on expert experience.
Assessment using numerical, data-driven values such as dollar amounts and probabilities; it takes more time and data but supports precise cost-benefit decisions.
The probability that a risk event will occur.
The severity of consequences if a risk event occurs.
Calculated as Likelihood multiplied by Impact.
A visual grid plotting likelihood on the Y-axis and impact on the X-axis, color-coded green, yellow, and red, to communicate risk exposure and guide resource decisions.
Avoid (eliminate the risk entirely), Mitigate (reduce the likelihood or impact), Transfer (shift the risk to a third party), and Accept (acknowledge and monitor without action).
Metrics and dashboards used to monitor and control risk responses.
An organization-wide framework of policies, processes, and capabilities that prepare a business to prevent, respond to, and recover from disruptive incidents.
The documented set of procedures an organization follows to keep critical functions running during, and immediately after, a disruption.
A technical, IT-focused subset of continuity planning concerned with restoring systems, data, and infrastructure after an outage.
The maximum acceptable time to restore a business function after a disruption occurs.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as the point in time to which data must be restored.

Also called Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption (MTPD); the longest period a critical function can be unavailable before consequences become unacceptable and survival is threatened. It is the outer boundary, not a target.
The time needed after systems are restored to verify data and resume normal processing.
The minimum service level the business must maintain during a disruption.

A process to identify and evaluate the effects of a disruption to critical business operations; it answers what happens financially, operationally, legally, and reputationally if a process stops working.
Any single component whose failure stops the entire process.
The ability to absorb and adapt to disruption without losing function.
The sustained delivery of a organization's critical services and functions throughout a disruption, not merely their eventual restoration.
The cycle of Plan, Test, Review results, and Update the plan with lessons learned to prove the plan before a real event does.
A backup that copies everything; it is the slowest to create, fastest to restore, and uses the most storage.
A backup that copies only data changed since the last backup of any kind; it is fast and storage-efficient but slower to restore because multiple sets are needed.
A backup that copies all data changed since the last full backup; it restores faster than incremental backups because only the full backup and latest differential are needed.
A real-time copy of the source data that does not keep older versions; if a file is deleted from the source, it is also removed from the mirror.
A documented plan developed in the Preparation phase that defines roles and responsibilities and removes guesswork about who does what during an incident.
A prepared kit containing forensic drives, cables, and checklists so the team can act immediately during an incident.
The stage where the team separates true security incidents from false alarms and determines the scope, nature, and severity of the event.

Notification (alert the right people through the right channels), Response (contain the incident, stop the damage, eliminate the root cause), and Recovery (restore systems and data, verify integrity, resume operations).
The response action that stops an incident from spreading while preserving evidence, such as isolating systems, disabling compromised accounts, and applying short-term fixes.
A method for finding the real cause by repeatedly asking why until reaching something that can actually be fixed.
Mean Time To Detect, a number tracked after an incident to measure how long it took to notice the problem.
Mean Time To Repair, a number tracked after an incident to measure how long it took to fix the problem.
Documenting findings as they are discovered during an incident so the evidence trail is preserved for further analysis.

The Philippine law requiring notification of the National Privacy Commission and affected persons within 72 hours of knowing or having reason to believe a breach happened, with a full breach report due within 5 days.
The circular implementing the Data Privacy Act's breach notification rules; the 72-hour and 5-day deadlines do not stop when an exemption is requested.
